about: Château Coutet is one of the great names of sweet Bordeaux and the largest vineyard in Barsac, with 38.5 hectares. Its square stone tower dates from the late thirteenth century, when the site was an English fort, and the name is said to come from the Gascon word for knife, a nod to the wine’s fresh, cutting acidity. Coutet has made sweet wine since 1643, belonged for more than a century to the Lur-Saluces family of Château d’Yquem, and was ranked a Premier Cru in the 1855 Classification. The Baly family has owned it since 1977, with Baron Philippe de Rothschild as exclusive distributor since 1994.

Barsac wines depend on noble rot, the botrytis fungus that shrivels ripe grapes in autumn mists rising from the Ciron and Garonne rivers and concentrates their sugar and acidity. In 2016 the fog arrived in the last week of September and botrytis followed. Ninety pickers went through the vineyard eight times between 30 September and 8 November, choosing only affected berries. The wine was fermented entirely in barrel and aged 18 months in French oak, half of it new, before bottling at the château in June 2018.

The 2016 is a blend of Sémillon with Sauvignon Blanc and a touch of Muscadelle. The estate notes orange and grapefruit, pineapple, peach, vanilla, broom flower and toasted brioche, on a powerful yet fresh palate; critics added honey, marmalade, candied orange peel and praline. It was one of the most highly praised sweet wines of a strong vintage.
